entities.name: Symbolic AI and expert systems
entities.criterion: A passage names, by one of the usual names listed, the approach of building intelligent programs from explicitly represented symbols, rules or encoded expert knowledge manipulated by inference; for a definition, it says what such a system or practice is.

search.venues: IJCAI proceedings index pages 1969, 1971, 1973, 1975 and 1977 (ijcai.org; titles searched for 'expert', 'knowledge-based', 'knowledge engineer', 'symbol'); full texts of the retrieved papers and reports listed in sources (RAND P-868 and P-1584 read as page images for their summaries and opening pages only); Buchanan and Shortliffe 1984, chapter 1.
search.years: 1956–1984 among the retrieved texts; title search 1969–1977.
search.methods: Regex search of the retrieved text layers for the listed names; title search of the IJCAI indexes; reading of the scanned RAND papers' first pages as images.
search.gaps: Only titles were searched in the IJCAI indexes, not full texts; the DENDRAL reports of 1969–1971 (Machine Intelligence volumes), Shortliffe's 1974 thesis and the 1976 MYCIN book, Stanford Heuristic Programming Project memos, and the Newell and Simon 1976 lecture ('physical symbol system') were not read; Haugeland 1985 ('GOFAI') is a book not retrieved. Buchanan and Shortliffe (1984) state that 'expert system' and 'knowledge-based system' came into general use about 1975, so earlier uses are likely to exist.
search.failures: dl.acm.org (Newell and Simon 1976, HTTP 403); cs.utexas.edu copy (TLS failure, then HTTP 503); amturing.acm.org (HTTP 403); sciencedirect.com (Lindsay et al. 1993 DENDRAL retrospective and Campbell et al. 2002 Deep Blue, HTTP 403).

corrections.reason: Same-family audit: Malhotra’s paper cites his MIT Sloan thesis of February 1975, “Design Requirements for a Knowledge-Based English Language System for Management: An Experimental Analysis” (reference 4, not read), which is earlier than the September 1975 conference; Buchanan and Shortliffe (1984) say the names came into general use about 1975, and the 1969–1974 Stanford DENDRAL and MYCIN reports were not searched.

entities.note: Family candidate. Its earliest located naming record is for the name "knowledge-based system"; no record says the family began there.

withheld.reason: Malhotra’s paper cites his MIT Sloan thesis of February 1975, “Design Requirements for a Knowledge-Based English Language System for Management: An Experimental Analysis” (reference 4, not read), which is earlier than the September 1975 conference; Buchanan and Shortliffe (1984) say the names came into general use about 1975, and the 1969–1974 Stanford DENDRAL and MYCIN reports were not searched.

entities.name: Search and planning
entities.criterion: A passage names search (the exploration of a space of possible solutions, usually guided by heuristics) or planning (constructing a sequence of actions or steps to reach a goal) as a method, technique or area of machine problem solving; for a definition, it says what the method is.

search.venues: RAND papers P-868 (1956) and P-1584 (1958/1959) read as page images (cover, summary and first pages only); Minsky 1961 (MIT transcription, full text); IJCAI proceedings index pages 1969–1977 (titles) and the full texts of Sandewall 1969 and Fikes and Nilsson 1971; Hart, Nilsson and Raphael 1968 (pages 1 and 3 as images); Lighthill 1972/1973 (Part I).
search.methods: Reading of the scanned first pages; regex search of text layers for "search", "planning", "heuristic search", "heuristic programming"; IJCAI title search.
search.gaps: The scanned Logic Theory Machine paper (64 pages) and the GPS report (29 pages) were read only on their opening pages, so an earlier use of "search" or "planning" in the 1956 paper is not excluded. Dartmouth-era texts in the dataset were not re-read for this family. Pre-1956 operations-research and game-tree texts (for example Shannon on chess programs) were not searched.
search.failures: rand.org PDF paths for P-1584 (HTTP 404, then 403); ai.stanford.edu copy of the A* paper (connection reset).

corrections.reason: Same-family audit: Simon and Newell, “Heuristic Problem Solving: The Next Advance in Operations Research” (Operations Research 6(1), 1958), names heuristic problem solving in its title and is earlier; it was not read. The 1956 Logic Theory Machine report (RAND P-868) was read only on its opening page images and has no text layer, and the 1956–1957 Logic Theory papers in the IRE Transactions and the Western Joint Computer Conference were not reached.

withheld.reason: Simon and Newell, “Heuristic Problem Solving: The Next Advance in Operations Research” (Operations Research 6(1), 1958), names heuristic problem solving in its title and is earlier; it was not read. The 1956 Logic Theory Machine report (RAND P-868) was read only on its opening page images and has no text layer, and the 1956–1957 Logic Theory papers in the IRE Transactions and the Western Joint Computer Conference were not reached.

claims.subject: th-newell-shaw-simon-1959-gps
claims.statement: Newell, Shaw and Simon's report on the General Problem Solver names means-ends analysis and planning as the two general problem-solving techniques in the program's repertoire.

time.note: Report dated 30 December 1958; the summary page that carries the passage is stamped 2-9-59 (revision of 9 February 1959).

claims.qualification: Held the earliest-located role in the draft; the role is withheld on 2026-10-29 (see the concept's note). Found by the recorded search; not evidence that the names began here. The passage names planning as a technique of one program, not a research field. The 1956 Logic Theory Machine paper was read only on its opening pages. Wording attested from the revised summary page of 9 February 1959.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 2 (report p. ii), Summary, item 3
evidence.passage: The summary lists among the program's major features 'The two general problem-solving techniques that now constitute its repertoire: means-ends analysis, and planning.'
evidence.note: Transcribed from the page image (no text layer); wording in single quotation marks is as read from the image.

claims.subject: minsky-1961-steps
claims.statement: Minsky's 'Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence' names Search and Planning among the five main areas into which it divides the problems of heuristic programming.
claims.qualification: Use. The summary is quoted from a later HTML transcription; the printed Proceedings of the IRE text was not compared.

evidence.locator: Summary (editorial summary at head of paper)
evidence.passage: The problems of heuristic programming—of making computers solve really difficult problems—are divided into five main areas: Search, Pattern-Recognition, Learning, Planning, and Induction.

claims.subject: th-sandewall-1969-heuristic-search
claims.statement: Sandewall's IJCAI 1969 paper presents itself as a survey and synthesis of past work on heuristic search methods.
claims.qualification: Use; the earliest title containing 'heuristic search' among the IJCAI indexes searched (1969–1977), which is not a claim about the phrase's earliest use.

evidence.passage: This paper is an attempt at a survey and synthesis of past work on heuristic search methods.

claims.subject: th-fikes-nilsson-1971-strips
claims.statement: Fikes and Nilsson's STRIPS paper lists 'robot planning' and 'heuristic search' among its descriptive terms.
claims.qualification: Use.

evidence.passage: robot planning, heuristic search.

claims.subject: minsky-1961-steps
claims.statement: Minsky (1961) describes the problem of search as testing possible answers to a problem against a means of checking a proposed solution, and values any device that reduces the search.
claims.qualification: Defining statement from a later HTML transcription; not evidence that the family began here.

evidence.locator: Section I, The Problem of Search, summary
evidence.passage: If, for a given problem, we have a means for checking a proposed solution, then we can solve the problem by testing all possible answers. But this always takes much too long to be of practical interest. Any device that can reduce this search may be of value.

claims.subject: th-hart-nilsson-raphael-1968-astar
claims.statement: Hart, Nilsson and Raphael (1968) describe how heuristic information from the problem domain can be incorporated into a formal mathematical theory of graph searching, and state an optimality property for a class of search strategies.
claims.qualification: Defining statement of the paper's approach, read from the scanned abstract; the optimality property is the paper's own claim, not checked here. The algorithm is named 'A*' in section II.

evidence.passage: The abstract states that the paper describes how heuristic information from the problem domain can be incorporated into a formal mathematical theory of graph searching, and demonstrates an optimality property of a class of search strategies.
evidence.note: Read from the page image; no text layer.

evidence.passage: The search procedure is set out under the heading 'Search Algorithm A*'.

claims.subject: th-sandewall-1969-heuristic-search
claims.statement: Sandewall (1969), following Feigenbaum and Feldman (1963), defines a heuristic method as a device that drastically limits search for solutions in large problem spaces.
claims.qualification: The definition is attributed by the paper to Feigenbaum and Feldman (1963), which was not retrieved.

evidence.passage: Following Feigenbaum and Feldman (1963), we define a heuristic method as a device which drastically limits search for solutions in large problem spaces.

claims.subject: th-fikes-nilsson-1971-strips
claims.statement: Fikes and Nilsson (1971) describe STRIPS as a problem solver that searches a space of world models for a sequence of operators transforming an initial model into one in which a goal formula can be proven.
claims.qualification: Description of one system's method, as its authors state it.

evidence.passage: We describe a new problem solver called STRIPS that attempts to find a sequence of operators in a space of world models to transform a given initial world model into a model in which a given goal formula can be proven to be true.

claims.subject: th-lighthill-1973-general-survey
claims.statement: Lighthill's survey singles out failure to recognise the implications of the combinatorial explosion as one general cause of the disappointments he reports in AI research.

time.note: Survey dated July 1972; published by the Science Research Council in 1973.

claims.qualification: Lighthill's assessment, which he presents as his personal view; it records what the survey says, not that the assessment is correct. Replies by Sutherland, Needham, Longuet-Higgins and Michie in the same paper symposium were not read.

evidence.passage: he is inclined, as a mathematician, to single out one rather general cause for the disappointments that have been experienced: failure to recognise the implications of the combinatorial explosion.

claims.subject: th-malhotra-1975-knowledge-based
claims.statement: Malhotra's IJCAI 1975 paper uses 'knowledge-based system' for a computer system whose work depends on domain knowledge attached to it and added over time.
claims.qualification: Held the earliest-located role in the draft; the role is withheld on 2026-10-29 (see the concept's note). Found by the recorded search (titles of the IJCAI proceedings 1969–1977 and the full texts retrieved); not evidence that the name began here. Buchanan and Shortliffe (1984) say the phrase came into general use about 1975, so earlier uses are likely; the 1969–1974 Stanford DENDRAL and MYCIN texts were not read.

evidence.passage: A knowledge-based system implies continuous modification.
KNOWLEDGE-BASED ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYSTEMS FOR MANAGEMENT SUPPORT: AN ANALYSIS OF REQUIREMENTS

openQuestions.question: Should the person credited by Kowalski (1988) with suggesting the name 'Prolog' ("Roussel's wife, Jacqueline") get a person record?
openQuestions.recommended: No: keep a literal object naming her as printed. She appears only in this attributed statement; a person record adds nothing and she is not otherwise a public actor in the dataset.

openQuestions.question: The discusses records use attributes.technical.kind values beyond 'definition' ('description' for a text's account of its own system, 'assessment' for Lighthill's judgement). Accept these kinds or fold them into 'definition'?
openQuestions.recommended: Accept 'description' and 'assessment' as distinct kinds: calling ELIZA's or Deep Blue's self-description a definition of a family would overstate it.

openQuestions.question: Is Kowalski 1974's 'predicate logic programming' (acknowledgment) and title 'Predicate Logic as Programming Language' close enough to hold earliest-located-term for 'logic programming'?
openQuestions.recommended: Yes, provisionally, with the qualification as written; the cross-family check should try to retrieve Kowalski's November 1973 DCL Memo 70 and the 1972 Jablonna paper, which could displace it.

openQuestions.question: Should the search-and-planning family hold its earliest-located record on GPS (1958/1959, "planning" as a technique) when the 1956 Logic Theory Machine paper was read only on its opening pages?
openQuestions.recommended: Yes, as stated in the search block; ask the cross-family checker to read P-868 in full for "search" and "planning" and to move the role if an earlier use meets the criterion.

openQuestions.question: The ELIZA, A*, STRIPS and Lighthill documents are marked timeline: true; the Sandewall, Malhotra and Mark papers only support naming records and are marked timeline: false. Is that the right split?
openQuestions.recommended: Yes; the timeline should carry systems, reports and papers of documentary standing, not every naming text.
